title: George Shearing's early style
summary: He recalls Shearing arriving from England and developing his style.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: I'd like to move on to some individuals to happen in this country, well known -- people who were well known, and have you talk a bit about your feelings on their music, the good side and the bad side (inaudible) and so on.
Let's start with George Shearing, who made a kind of a --

Well, to me, -- I'm glad you brought that, too. I look at that man and I picture him in two different pictures. When I say two different pictures, I met the man (inaudible) came from England. And I know how he played. When he got here, the man that (unintelligible) at 52nd, where
George used to hang around every night for open to close, was Earl Gardner.

Earl Gardner. Shearing didn't even play the way he plays now, the way he played after he made a success. He stopped fooling around and developed something. That was his way of playing piano when he came here from England.
Yeah, I've got one old trio recording he made before he ever came here, which was basically a piano style.
I know, exactly. That's exactly what I'm driving at.

It was so -- when I heard George Shearing again, and we were working the Everly Club, he hired a group that was him, (unintelligible) on the clarinet, this bass player that was his manager after awhile, what was his name? Colored guy. What was his name, the bass player? He became to be his personal manager. What's the guy's name now? Well, it was a quartet. Then I heard a different George Shearing.
How about when he started teaming up with the Latin percussionist?
And then from there, now he already accumulating what he heard at 52nd, he developed something.
He started rising. He used to play behind the stage with a lead accordion. He used to write something and Buddy Defranco was on the scene, playing all that stuff and they created a sound.
